1.pericope_label: the law given to Moses and Aaron together, and why it exists

schools.summary: Ellicott sees the LORD honouring Aaron, lately rebuked, by addressing both conjointly; Keil and Delitzsch set the chapter among the instructions about what hinders fellowship with God, sin having spread from man to the whole creation.

Gill divides the office between chief magistrate and high priest and includes health among the reasons; Calvin flatly refuses the medical reading, insisting the law was elementary instruction whose body is Christ.
Henry gives four reasons — God's bare will, the unwholesomeness of the meats, separation from idolatrous neighbours, and the loathing of creatures the heathen venerated.

Clarke links the chapter back to the priests' prohibition of wine and quotes Bishop Wilson that no art of man could have held a nation to such precepts; Wesley divides the duty between priest and magistrate and includes health.

debates.question: Did God have the people's health in view in these laws?

sides.position: yes, among other reasons — most of the forbidden meats were really unwholesome
no — to make God a physician here perverts the whole force of the law, whose object was holiness

schools.summary: Ellicott requires the hoof divided below as much as above, excluding the dog and the cat; Keil and Delitzsch derive the word for rumination and note the two clauses are joined so that both marks must hold.

Gill insists the hoof must be cloven quite through; Calvin reports the old allegory of discernment and meditation, refuses the mystical subtlety added to it, and then admits he does not know why these two marks were chosen.
Clarke describes the four stomachs of the ox and the purpose of rumination; Wesley says both properties are necessary and the reason must be resolved into the lawgiver's will.

debates.question: Do the two marks signify anything beyond themselves?

sides.position: yes — discernment and meditation, or good works and good affections, and neither will do alone
the ground of the choice is finally unknown, and the mystical readings have licensed every imagination

4.pericope_label: the four exceptions, and the ban on touching the carcase

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the concessive construction in each case, describes the camel's elastic pad, defends the rabbit against the hyrax, and gathers the evidence for the horror of swine; Keil and Delitzsch concede that the hare and hyrax are not true ruminants and conclude that Moses followed the popular opinion.
Gill states the principle that one mark without the other will not serve; Calvin makes it a rule that partial purity must not be obtruded on God, and explains why the swine bit hardest.
Clarke identifies the coney with the daman and lists the swine's vices; Wesley calls camel usual food in Arabia and denies that the ban on touching is absolute.

debates.question: Do the coney and the hare really chew the cud?

sides.position: not truly — they lack the ruminant stomach, but appear to masticate, and Moses used the marks in common vogue
not the rabbit but the daman of Judea and Arabia
the rabbit, as the men who administered the law in Palestine understood it
the Syrian hyrax or rock-badger

themes: the camel, coney, hare and swine

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that no fish is named and the rule left generic for the administrators, and gives their four criteria; Keil and Delitzsch exclude crabs and scaleless fish and cite Numa's parallel law.
Gill reports the Egyptian priests' abstinence and Julian's reasons; Calvin again refuses the medical reading and explains the absence of names by the poverty of Jewish rivers.
Henry reads the permission as generous, God allowing his servants not only for necessity but for delight, and limits the abomination to Jews.
Clarke blames the glutinous flesh of scaleless fish; Wesley adds that the fish were never brought to Adam to be named, and that "unto you" marks a distinction meant to cease.

debates.question: Why does the law name no fish at all?

sides.position: most were unknown to a people with almost no rivers
they had no names, never having been brought to Adam
the rule was deliberately generic, to be defined by those who administered it

13.pericope_label: the birds: the first part of the register

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the four second-Temple marks of an unclean bird, identifies the ossifrage as the lammergeier, corrects the claim that the eagle disdains carrion, and gives up on the night hawk; Keil and Delitzsch count twenty varieties and pass on Knobel's judgement that the list is not exhaustive.
Gill reports Maimonides' count of twenty-four and reads the fourth name as ostrich on the authority of the versions.
Henry sorts the forbidden birds into predators, solitaries, feeders on impurity, and birds used in divination.
Clarke works from the roots of the names and reports the rival identifications; Wesley reaches nearly the same heads as Henry and takes the loss of the vocabulary as a sign that the law has ceased.

debates.question: What is the fourth bird, which the English calls an owl?

sides.position: the ostrich, with the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Targums
the male ostrich
the Oriental owl
undeterminable — leave the Authorised Version alone

17.pericope_label: the birds: the rest of the register, down to the bat

schools.summary: Ellicott argues from the parallel list in Deuteronomy that this verse has been disturbed, explains why two owls are named separately, denies the swan outright, and reads the last three birds by their names — the merciful, the pious, and the angry.
Gill reports Ainsworth's reversal of the first and last names, describes the great horned owl, and tells the story of the storks in the fire at Delft.
Clarke derives each name from its root, prefers the diver for the cormorant, and supplies the heron's temper from his own knowledge of one that nearly killed a man.

debates.question: Has the order of this verse been disturbed?

sides.position: yes — Deuteronomy places the cormorant sixth, which leaves the two owls together

20.pericope_label: the winged creeping things, and the locusts excepted

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that "upon all four" counts feet, follows the inclusion of the bee into the question whether its honey is clean, and gives the four marks of an edible locust; Keil and Delitzsch identify the exception as locusts while admitting the species cannot be fixed.
Gill lists the creatures meant — flies, fleas, bees, wasps, hornets, locusts.
Henry notes that several sorts of locust were good meat and much used, and that John the Baptist lived on them.

Clarke denies the third name can be a beetle, since no beetle was ever eaten anywhere, and reports Shaw eating locusts fried and salted; Wesley finds a moral in a flying thing that crawls, and lists the nations that ate them.

debates.question: Is the honey of bees unclean, the bee being among the creeping things?

sides.position: no — it is not the direct produce of the insect but a preparation from the juices of clean herbs, and was expressly permitted
the honey of the promised land must therefore have been grape-honey or a vegetable exudation

24.pericope_label: defilement by touching or carrying a carcase

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch grade the defilement, touching from carrying; Ellicott fixes the day at sunset, reports the rule that washing clothes always included bathing, and sets out the Pharisee and Sadducee reading of the pronoun.
Gill glosses the defilement as incurred by eating or removing them.

Henry denies that these carcases defiled the conscience, notes that somebody must touch them to remove them, and finds in the evening limit a sign that ceremonial pollution would end with the death of Christ.
Clarke identifies the beasts that go on their paws; Wesley states the exclusion from the court of God's house and from free conversation.

debates.question: Does a living unclean animal defile, or only its carcase?

sides.position: only the carcase — which is why camels, asses and horses were freely used
the living animal too, so that touching any beast in this list defiled

29.pericope_label: the eight creeping things that defile

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies each from the second-Temple descriptions, rules out the tortoise in favour of the toad, and reads the opening phrase as "the most unclean"; Keil and Delitzsch admit the names are still undecided, and deny the phrase means these were more unclean — only that they were likelier to fall dead into a pot.
Gill records the later rule that with such a creature the blood defiles as the flesh does.
Clarke prefers the mole to the weasel and reads most of the rest as lizards.

debates.question: Why are these eight singled out?

sides.position: they are pre-eminently unclean among creeping things
they are no more unclean than the rest, but live in houses and so are far likelier to fall dead on utensils and food

debates.question: What is the third creature, rendered tortoise?

sides.position: the toad — the tortoise is expressly not defiling, and it is the toad that can be mistaken for a frog
a crocodile, frog or toad; certainly not the tortoise

32.pericope_label: what a carcase defiles: vessels, clothing, food and ovens

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the vessel that can be washed from the earthen one that must be broken, and reject the traditional rendering of the clause about water on grammatical grounds; Ellicott defines each material narrowly and reports the rule that only a portion with flesh on it defiles.
Gill notes that dry bones, nails and skin separated from the creature do not defile.
Clarke furnishes the furniture of an Arab tent and describes the ranges for pots as a hole dug in the floor; Wesley distinguishes food dressed in water from food eaten dry.

debates.question: What does the clause about water mean?

sides.position: food prepared with water — the Hebrew cannot mean "such water", i.e. water out of the defiled vessel
food on which any of seven liquids has been poured, which stays liable even after drying
food dressed in water in a polluted vessel, but not food eaten dry

36.pericope_label: the exemptions: springs, cisterns, and seed for sowing

schools.summary: Ellicott grounds both exemptions on constant change — the fresh supply in a cistern and the new moisture a growing plant draws — and states the mercy of the provision where water is scarce; Keil and Delitzsch say the uncleanness on dry seed would simply be absorbed by the earth, while softened grain would carry it into the fruit.
Gill takes the fountain and pit as one large continence of water.

Wesley grounds the exemption on the lawgiver's merciful condescension to men's necessities, and draws from it that God would have the ceremonial law give place to the law of mercy; Clarke explains it by running water and large reservoirs purifying themselves.

39.pericope_label: the clean beast that dies of itself

schools.summary: Ellicott defines the case as a clean animal not properly slaughtered, limits the defilement to the flesh so that skins and horns remained usable for scrolls and trumpets, and reads the eating as done ignorantly; Keil and Delitzsch set the grading beside the earlier rule.
Gill names the animals concerned and marks that what would have been lawful is not lawful now.
Wesley adds the beast killed by a wild beast and puts his finger on what is common to both, that the blood was not poured forth; and reserves wilful eating for excision.

fidelity.note: the closing paragraph, setting the whole chapter's remediable ceremonial defilement against the excision reserved for deliberate contempt, is the summary's own framing; the excision itself is Ellicott's and Wesley's point on this verse

41.pericope_label: the creeping things forbidden as food

schools.summary: Ellicott sorts the creeping things into three classes and reports the exemption of worms bred inside food; Keil and Delitzsch note the enlarged letter marking the middle of the Pentateuch.

Gill supplies the definition of a creeping thing and records that serpents have all the same been eaten; Calvin denies the chapter has health in view at all, grounds holiness in the nature of God, and compares a religion of bare observances to learning the alphabet and never joining the letters to read.
Clarke reports the Masoretic note on the middle letter of the law; Wesley matches the three classes to worms, snakes and toads.

themes: the middle letter of the law
the alphabet never joined into words

44.pericope_label: be ye holy, for I am holy

schools.summary: Ellicott grounds the whole law in the holiness of the God who gave it, notes the apostolic reuse of the very words, and gathers the scriptural appeals to the deliverance from Egypt.
Gill takes the double title, Lord and God, as at once a right to command and a pledge to consult their good.
Henry rules out both the bill of fare and the physician's prescription, names the three things the law was to teach, and reads the deliverance from Egypt as an argument from gratitude.

Clarke insists the forbidden meats really were injurious and God a tender father in banning them, yet ends on holiness as the grand design, and argues from the lost vocabulary that the law must be considered abrogated; Wesley denies there was any real uncleanness in the creatures at all.

debates.question: Was there any real uncleanness in the forbidden creatures?

sides.position: none whatever — the rules were to train them away from moral pollution
yes — they were genuinely injurious to body and mind, and God banned them as a father does what will make his children sick

themes: brought you up out of Egypt

46.pericope_label: the colophon: that ye may put difference

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the summary reorders the four classes, as the sacrificial colophon also does, renders the purpose "that ye may put difference", and reports the ruling drawn from the unqualified word for beast; Keil and Delitzsch carry the closing formula.
Gill sums up the chapter as equipping Israel to tell the one from the other.

Henry calls it a statute for ever only as long as that economy lasted, points to the voice from heaven that repealed it, and closes with three applications — thanksgiving, standing fast in liberty, and a self-imposed temperance.
Wesley says the same of its repeal and bids us bless God that every creature is now good.

themes: repealed by a voice from heaven
